endorsements.quote: Because dementia symptoms progressively reduce independence and decision‐making capacity, it is essential to actively involve people with dementia in the design process using participatory methods that respect their autonomy.

For high‐risk applications, the workgroup recommends establishing continuous communication and evaluation loops with ethicists, technical developers, clinicians, caregivers, and users to refine AI tools based on lived experience.

Involve a diverse range of stakeholders, including people with ADRD, caregivers, healthcare providers, ethicists, business professionals, and technical developers, in the integration of AI systems from the early stages.
This calls for developers to produce plain‐language summaries alongside technical reports when AI systems are introduced into healthcare settings.
Moreover, education efforts should extend to caregivers and family members, who often act as intermediaries and decision makers.
They are expected to explain the purpose, benefits, risks, and limitations of these technologies to patients and caregivers – just as they do with traditional medical interventions.

Sponsors are urged to characterize datasets, analyze performance by subgroups (e.g., race, sex, age), address limitations through ongoing monitoring and updates, and transparently report known biases, supporting equitable and effective device performance throughout its lifecycle.

To maintain fairness (equitable performance across patient subgroups) and reliability (consistent performance over time), teams should define explicit, pre‐specified performance “re‐audit triggers,” established during development and calibrated to the tool's risk tier.
Developers should launch small, well‐monitored pilots with pre‐defined criteria for expansion, modification, or discontinuation.

The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) recommends reducing bias in AI‐enabled medical devices by ensuring representation across relevant demographic groups during data collection, development, and validation.

To ensure that development safeguards match the level of potential harm without unnecessarily slowing innovation, we propose aligning our risk categorization with the four‐tier framework established by the EU AI Act, which classifies AI systems by potential harm into unacceptable, high, limited, and minimal risk categories.
We recommend budgeting for ethical oversight during project planning to ensure it is treated as an integral part of the development process.

unlisted_practices: Require human review before any automated action for AI systems generating high-risk predictions such as fall risk or agitation.
Display uncertainty ranges in interfaces and prompt users to confirm recommendations to mitigate automation bias.
Reassess decision-making capacity of people living with dementia through periodic validated assessments at defined intervals or clinical milestones rather than a single baseline.
Trigger adaptive safeguards, including progressive shift of consent authority to designated caregivers, when capacity decline is documented.
Prohibit AI that exploits cognitive vulnerability to manipulate decisions or behavior or enables surveillance without meaningful consent.
Designate at least one team member as ethics lead and publish an ethical code of conduct.
Use federated learning and modality-tiered privacy rules to minimize sharing of identifiable data.
Inform users and caregivers clearly that they are interacting with an AI system.
Provide ethics and responsible innovation training to all stakeholders involved in AI development.
Link AI ethical principles to measurable real-world goals such as earlier diagnosis, quality of life, and reduced caregiver burden.
Balance the risks of premature deployment against the harms of delaying beneficial AI tools.

screen.reason: This is a perspective article presenting a consensus framework and strategic pathway (recommendations/guidelines) for ethical development and deployment of AI tools in dementia care.
